candidate_sources.title: Cercospora Leaf Spot and Berry Blotch - Welcome Coffee Growers!
candidate_sources.snippet: Cercospora leaf spot and berry blotch of coffee caused by Cercospora coffeicola. Covers symptoms on leaves (brown spots with light grey centres and dark brown ring) and berries (sunken tan lesions with ashy center that penetrate to the bean affecting quality and taste). Premature ripening of diseased cherries is a key symptom. Extension resource from Hawaii coffee education program.

candidate_sources.title: Cercospora coffeicola; Brown eye spot, Berry blotch - Plantwise Knowledge Bank
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI Plantwise datasheet on Cercospora coffeicola covering brown eye spot and berry blotch of coffee. Includes identity, distribution, hosts/species affected, diagnosis, biology and ecology. Reddish dark brown patchy lesions on berries (berry blotch) similar to coffee berry disease but not sunken. Disease occurs across Asia, Africa, Americas, Caribbean, and Oceania.

candidate_sources.title: Coffee brown-eye spot (142) - Pacific Pests, Pathogens & Weeds Fact Sheet
candidate_sources.snippet: Fact sheet on coffee brown-eye spot caused by Cercospora coffeicola (sexual stage Mycosphaerella coffeicola). Small brown spots on leaves up to 15 mm with light brown centres, dark brown ring, and yellow margin. On berries, irregularly shaped brown sunken lesions with purple halo on green fruit; reddish dark brown patchy lesions (berry blotch). Yield losses up to 15% annually. Covers symptoms, management, and distribution.

candidate_sources.title: Black rot or koleroga - TNAU Agritech Portal
candidate_sources.snippet: Black rot or koleroga of coffee caused by Koleroga noxia (syn. Corticium koleroga, Pellicularia koleroga). Seasonal disease mainly confined to rainy season, generally noticed in valley areas of plantations. Attacks leaves, twigs and berries. Affected leaves get detached from branches and hang down by means of slimy fungal strands. Blackening and rotting of infected leaves, developing berries and young twigs.

candidate_sources.title: Fact sheet - Coffee thread blight (199) - Pacific Pests Pathogens & Weeds
candidate_sources.snippet: Coffee thread blight or koleroga or black rot caused by Ceratobasidium noxium (syn. Corticium koleroga). The fungus forms mats and threads of light-coloured growth on the underside of leaves and twigs. At first, leaves appear light grey and dry. Later, the leaves blacken and fall. Affects coffee, black pepper, citrus, ginger, tea. Includes symptoms, management, and lifecycle information.

candidate_sources.title: Understanding and Managing Black Rot Disease in Coffee - Agriculture Institute
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive guide on black rot disease of coffee caused by Koleroga noxia. Covers symptoms on leaves, shoots, stems and berries: small dark spots expanding and turning jet black, young shoots turning completely black within days, infected shoots becoming brittle. Environmental conditions: high humidity exceeding 80%, temperatures 20-28°C. Includes cultural and chemical management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Fact sheet - Coffee brown-eye spot (142)
candidate_sources.snippet: Circular brown spots, mostly 5-10 mm, with bright grey centres and yellow haloes, are typical of brown-eye leaf spot. Caused by Cercospora coffeicola. High humidity, rain, warm temperatures and drought stress after flowering all favour the disease. Management includes spacing, nitrogen and potassium nutrition, shade, pruning, copper fungicides and triazoles.

candidate_sources.title: Cercospora Leaf Spot and Berry Blotch of Coffee (PD-41)
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension factsheet from University of Hawaii CTAHR covering Cercospora coffeicola symptoms on leaves and berries, disease cycle, and management of coffee cercospora leaf spot and berry blotch.

candidate_sources.title: Mycosphaerella coffeicola (brown eye spot of coffee) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI datasheet on Mycosphaerella coffeicola (Cercospora coffeicola), the causal agent of brown eye spot of coffee, with detailed symptoms, distribution, biology, and management information.

candidate_sources.title: Perileucoptera coffeella (coffee leaf miner) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Datasheet on Perileucoptera coffeella (coffee leaf miner) covering Identity, Overview, Distribution, Hosts/Species Affected, Diagnosis, Biology & Ecology, Natural Enemies, Impacts, Prevention/Control. Coffee leaves infested with P. coffeella are recognized by large, irregular, brown spots on the upper surface of the leaf.

candidate_sources.title: Coffee Leaf Miner | Pests & Diseases - Plantix
candidate_sources.snippet: Symptoms include irregular brown spots on upper leaf surface, pale yellow trails under the coffee leaf epidermis, and large necrotic patches. Adults are tiny silvery-white moths (3-5 mm). Larvae are flat, pale-green caterpillars that mine between upper and lower epidermis of leaves, causing necrosis, defoliation, and yield loss of 30-70%.

candidate_sources.title: Coffee Leaf Miner - NKO - Hawaii Coffee Education
candidate_sources.snippet: Extension-style guide on coffee leaf miner (Leucoptera coffeella) identification, damage symptoms, and management for coffee growers. Covers signs of infestation, lifecycle, and control strategies including cultural practices and biological control.

candidate_sources.title: Phoma costarricensis (leaf blight: coffee) - CABI Invasive Species Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: CABI datasheet on Phoma costarricensis, the causal agent of coffee leaf blight. Covers identity, distribution, hosts, symptoms, biology, detection, and management of the pathogen on coffee.

candidate_sources.title: Phoma spot or ascochyta spot of coffee - Cultivar Magazine
candidate_sources.snippet: Phoma tarda is the main etiological agent of tip blight and phoma leaf spot on coffee plants in Brazil and Africa. Symptoms include tip and branch dieback, necrosis of rosettes, mummified berries and leaf spots. At temperatures below 20°C, relative humidity below 70% and strong winds, damage is more severe especially above 900m altitude. Control includes windbreaks, balanced fertilization with nitrogen, calcium and micronutrients, and chemical control when necessary.

candidate_sources.title: Ascochyta tarda - Wikipedia
candidate_sources.snippet: Ascochyta tarda (syn. Phoma tarda) is a fungal plant pathogen that causes dieback and leafspot on coffee, first observed in Ethiopia in 1954. Known as a noxious pathogen of arabica coffee in Ethiopia, Kenya, Cameroon and Southeast Asia. Infection favored at 15-20°C with increasing leaf wetness duration increasing sporulation. Cold climate, heavy rain, strong wind and hail increase probability of infection.

candidate_sources.title: Hemileia vastatrix (coffee leaf rust) | CABI Compendium
candidate_sources.snippet: Comprehensive datasheet covering identity, distribution, hosts, diagnosis, biology and ecology, impacts, and prevention/control of coffee leaf rust caused by Hemileia vastatrix. Rust lesions consist of many individual uredinia scattered on the underside of leaves. Covers race-specific and durable resistance in commercial cultivars.

candidate_sources.title: Coffee Leaf Rust - North Central Integrated Pest Management Center
candidate_sources.snippet: Pest alert on coffee leaf rust (Hemileia vastatrix). Describes symptoms including yellow-orange powdery spots on lower leaf surfaces, corresponding yellow patches on upper surface, early leaf shedding, and reduced photosynthesis. Covers pathogen biology, favorable conditions, and integrated pest management strategies.

candidate_sources.title: Coffee Rust: symptoms, causes, cycle and solutions
candidate_sources.snippet: Detailed guide on coffee rust (Hemileia vastatrix) covering symptoms (yellow-orange spots 2-3mm expanding to 4cm, powdery orange underside), disease cycle, environmental conditions favoring infection (16-28°C, free water), and management solutions including spacing, pruning, resistant cultivars (Catimor hybrids), and biological control.
